title: Investigating Online RL in World Models

raw.stage1:
### Purpose
The contribution aims to address the pathologies of model-based offline RL (value overestimation and limited out-of-sample exploration caused by short truncated rollouts) by enabling effective full-length rollout training without hand-crafted uncertainty penalties. Paper [7] ("MOPO: Model-based Offline Policy Optimization") and paper [16] ("MOReL: Model-Based Offline Reinforcement Learning") both discuss addressing value overestimation and distributional shift in offline RL, but they rely on hand-crafted penalties or constraints to mitigate these issues. Paper [23] ("Optimistic Model Rollouts for Pessimistic Offline Policy Optimization") also addresses similar pathologies but focuses on pessimistic Markov Decision Processes (P-MDPs) rather than enabling full-length rollouts without penalties. None of these papers propose the same purpose of enabling full-length rollouts without hand-crafted penalties.

### Mechanism
The mechanism involves training a recurrent policy through full-length offline rollouts inside learned world models, treating each member of a world-model ensemble as a level in the Unsupervised Environment Design (UED) framework to make full rollouts robust without hand-crafted penalties. Paper [4] ("Replay-Guided Adversarial Environment Design") and paper [6] ("Emergent Complexity and Zero-shot Transfer via Unsupervised Environment Design") both introduce the UED framework, but neither applies it to world-model ensembles or offline RL. Paper [9] ("Stabilizing Unsupervised Environment Design with a Learned Adversary") and paper [20] ("Grounding Aleatoric Uncertainty for Unsupervised Environment Design") further develop UED but focus on adaptive curricula and aleatoric uncertainty rather than robustness in full-length rollouts. Paper [16] ("MOReL") and paper [7] ("MOPO") discuss world-model ensembles but do not integrate UED or recurrent policies for full-length rollouts. Thus, the mechanism is uncovered.

### Evaluation
The evaluation matches online PPO performance on standard offline RL (D4RL) benchmarks while using fewer transitions than online algorithms are traditionally trained on and demonstrates transfer back to the original environment. Paper [17] ("D4RL: Datasets for Deep Data-Driven Reinforcement Learning") introduces the D4RL benchmark family, which is widely used in offline RL evaluations, including in papers [7], [16], [18], and [23]. These papers also evaluate offline RL algorithms using D4RL benchmarks and metrics like policy performance and transferability. The evaluation design (using D4RL benchmarks and comparing performance metrics) is therefore covered.

### Domain
The domain is reinforcement learning, specifically model-based offline RL using world models. Papers [7], [16], [23], and [18] all operate in the same general application area of model-based offline RL with world models. While the specific sub-problem (full-length rollouts without penalties) is new, the domain itself is not novel.

**PURPOSE**
The purpose is to address the standard pathologies of model-based offline RL, such as value overestimation and problems from distributional shift, which are caused by out-of-distribution actions during model rollouts. This general objective is shared by numerous prior works in the field. For example, [7] identifies the core problem as being "exceptionally difficult, due to the distributional shift between the offline training data and the learned policy," and [13] aims to solve "extrapolation error caused by the out-of-distribution (OOD) actions."

**MECHANISM**
The mechanism involves training a policy inside an ensemble of learned world models, but crucially, it treats each member of the world model ensemble as a distinct environment ("level") within the Unsupervised Environment Design (UED) framework. While prior work introduces UED (e.g., [6] proposes it as a paradigm where "environments with unknown parameters... are then automatically curated") and other work uses ensembles of world models for uncertainty quantification in offline RL (e.g., [7] uses "an ensemble of probabilistic dynamics models" to create a penalty), no prior paper combines these ideas by using the world model ensemble itself as the set of environments for UED to induce robustness.

**EVALUATION**
The evaluation design consists of measuring performance on the standard D4RL benchmark suite and comparing it to other algorithms, including online methods. This evaluation design is not new; the D4RL benchmark family was specifically introduced for this purpose in [17] ("D4RL: Datasets for Deep Data-Driven Reinforcement Learning"), and its use for benchmarking offline RL algorithms is a standard community practice, as exemplified by [18].

**DOMAIN**
The contribution operates in the domain of model-based offline reinforcement learning using world models. This is a well-established research area covered by many of the prior papers. For instance, [3] is "A Survey on Offline Model-Based Reinforcement Learning," and papers like [1], [2], [7], and [16] all explicitly work within this domain.

### Purpose
The contribution's purpose is to overcome the healthy-behavior/near-optimal bias documented in standard offline RL benchmarks (e.g., D4RL) that hampers the development of generalizable methods. Paper [2] explicitly discusses the imbalance in real-world offline RL datasets, where state coverage follows a power-law distribution characterized by skewed policies, which aligns with the documented bias in standard benchmarks. Paper [9] (D4RL) also acknowledges the limitations of existing offline RL benchmarks, including biases that hinder generalization, but does not specifically focus on overcoming them. Paper [7] empirically finds that datasets dominated by suboptimal trajectories lead to poor performance in offline RL, which is closely related to the stated purpose. Thus, [2] and [7] substantively cover the purpose.

### Mechanism
The contribution introduces a data curation method to produce a new dataset that does not exhibit the positive/healthy-state biases of previous benchmarks. Paper [13] proposes REPAIR, a dataset resampling procedure to minimize representation bias, which is conceptually equivalent to reducing biases in datasets. Paper [19] (BiaSwap) introduces a bias-tailored augmentation approach to remove dataset bias, which also aligns with the mechanism of curating datasets to mitigate bias. Both [13] and [19] contain substantively equivalent mechanisms.

### Evaluation
The contribution evaluates the dataset qualitatively by showing that conventional offline RL methods underperform on it while the proposed method remains robust, using it as a stress-test dataset in experiments. Paper [9] (D4RL) uses a similar evaluation design, where datasets are stress-tested by applying offline RL methods to assess their performance. Paper [5] (RL Unplugged) also evaluates offline RL benchmarks by testing methods on diverse datasets to compare robustness and generalization. Both [9] and [5] match the evaluation design.

### Domain
The contribution operates in the domain of reinforcement learning benchmarks/datasets. Papers [9], [5], [3], and [6] all work in the same general application area of offline RL benchmarks and datasets, even though they target different specific sub-problems or datasets. Thus, the domain is covered by multiple prior papers.

The stated purpose is to provide an algorithm leveraging an ensemble of world models to train a transferable policy using online-RL advances in an offline setting. Paper [1] discusses offline RL using world models but focuses on finetuning them in real-world robotic tasks, which is narrower than the stated purpose. Thus, the mechanism is partially covered by [14] for the UED sampling/selection aspect.

Paper [12] benchmarks offline RL algorithms using D3RLpy, which includes D4RL datasets and similar evaluation metrics. Paper [13] evaluates offline RL algorithms on D4RL benchmarks, which aligns with the evaluation design. The evaluation design is covered by these prior papers.

The domain is reinforcement learning (RL), specifically offline RL. Papers [1], [2], [3], [7], [8], [12], [13], and many others address offline RL, making the domain clearly covered.

## Purpose

The purpose is: "Provide a concrete algorithm that leverages an ensemble of world models to train a transferable policy using online-RL advances in an offline setting."

This combines: (1) ensemble of world models for offline RL, and (2) applying online-RL curriculum/UED advances to the offline setting. Paper [7] (MOReL) uses model-based offline RL with ensembles. Paper [3] uses probabilistic ensembles for model-based offline RL. Paper [9] argues offline RL policies should be adaptive (recurrent policy in offline setting). Paper [27] revisits design choices in model-based offline RL. The specific objective of "using online-RL advances (UED/curriculum) to train via world model ensembles offline" is partially touched by [26] (curriculum offline RL) and [3], but none specifically frame the purpose as "apply UED/online-RL advances to offline setting via world model ensemble." Paper [26] (Curriculum Offline RL) is closest to the purpose of applying curriculum learning to offline RL. However, the specific framing of using UED with world model ensembles as levels is not directly covered. Still, at the problem-class level, [3] and [7] cover "train policy using ensemble of world models in offline setting," and [26] covers "apply online-RL curriculum advances to offline RL." Together these cover the purpose. Paper [3] explicitly covers "model-based offline RL with ensemble world models."

## Mechanism

The mechanism is: POWER — trains a collection of world models, treats them as UED levels, and uses UED sampling methods (e.g., prioritized level replay) to select which world model the agent interacts with, while training a recurrent policy.

Paper [14] (Prioritized Level Replay) introduces PLR — prioritizing which environment levels to train on using regret/learning progress signals. Paper [24] introduces UED. Paper [29] (REPAIRED/Evolving Curricula) uses regret-based environment design. Paper [16] (Stabilizing UED) uses learned adversary for UED. The key novel primitive here is: treating world models as UED levels and applying PLR/UED sampling to select among them. No prior paper treats world models as UED levels. Paper [14] applies PLR to procedurally generated environment levels, not world models. This combination — world model ensemble + UED level selection — does not appear in any prior paper. The closest is [3] which uses ensemble world models for offline RL but with standard ensemble averaging/pessimism, not UED-style selection.

## Evaluation

The evaluation involves: (1) comparison against standard offline RL methods on a curated dataset, (2) comparison to online PPO on D4RL, (3) diversity analysis of world models. Paper [8] introduces D4RL — the benchmark used. Paper [12] benchmarks offline RL algorithms on D4RL. Papers [7], [3], [27] all evaluate on D4RL against offline RL baselines. The evaluation design (comparing offline RL methods on D4RL, measuring performance vs. online RL) is well-established in prior work [8], [12], [7], [3].

## Domain

The domain is reinforcement learning (algorithm). Virtually all prior papers [1]-[32] operate in the RL domain. This is clearly covered.
